Built Different: Are Litigators the Legal Industry’s Biggest Hurdle in AI Uptake? // Cooley // Global Law Firm
stories.ltme_summary: Cooley's chief innovation officer David Wang, quoted in Law.com, says litigators may be more cautious about AI because of fear, courtroom scrutiny and professional responsibility. He argues AI's value in litigation lies in better review, preparation and training rather than time saved. The page is a firm reprint with a subscription-only original.

The episode argues clients now arrive with AI answers and lawyers must help them judge reliability. The extract is a show description.
stories.hook: Hogan Lovells Cadwalader's Melissa Bianchi asks whether AI will erode junior lawyer judgment

stories.ltme_summary: Legl's product page says its Risk Rules feature tailors rules from a firm's written risk policy to its own standards. The page is a vendor description of a compliance tool for law firms.

stories.title: SRA AML annual report 2025/26: key takeaways for law firms | Legl
stories.ltme_summary: Legl has summarised the SRA's AML annual report for 2025/26, published on 22 October 2026. It reports that 78 per cent of firms inspected were compliant or partially compliant, and that non-compliance fell from 32.4 per cent to 21.9 per cent. The SRA's enforcement outcomes rose from 137 to 256, with AML fines of around £2.6m across the year.
stories.hook: Legl reads the SRA's AML report as showing firms have controls but weak file-level scrutiny of source of funds

stories.title: Orbital becomes first AI platform to license ALTA forms and survey standards | Orbital
stories.ltme_summary: Orbital, an AI platform for real estate legal work, says it has signed a multi-year content licence with the American Land Title Association to use ALTA Policy Forms, endorsements and the 2026 ALTA/NSPS survey standards inside its platform. Orbital says the deal covers more than 250,000 real estate transactions a year. The announcement is dated 10 November 2026.
stories.hook: Orbital licenses ALTA policy forms and survey standards for its real estate AI platform

stories.title: AI glossary for law firms
stories.ltme_summary: Smokeball has published a plain-English glossary of AI terms for law firms, covering terms such as hallucination, large language model and data privacy. It frames the list as a guide for evaluating tools and asking vendors sharper questions.
stories.hook: Smokeball publishes plain-English AI glossary aimed at law firm buyers

stories.title: Inside an AI-Native Legal Team

The extract is a single sentence, so the figures and team structure are not visible here. The publication date shown is 24 November, after the 16 November date of the batch.
stories.hook: Wordsmith says it will show its own AI-native legal team's numbers

stories.title: Are We About To Lose Another Major Firm? — See Generally
stories.ltme_summary: Above the Law's weekly roundup covers Biglaw news, including the wind-down of Weil, speculation over Cahill Gordon, Dechert hiring a former DOJ adviser, and a judge barring a federal prosecutor from a case. It also notes the death of Judge Richard Posner. The extract is a multi-item digest rather than a single report.
stories.hook: Above the Law's roundup links Weil's wind-down to Cahill Gordon speculation and Dechert hiring

stories.title: UK court support charity closes two services following funding cut
stories.ltme_summary: Support Through Court, a charity helping people who represent themselves in civil and family courts, has begun closing its services in Chelmsford and Southend after the Ministry of Justice cut its annual funding by £300,000, according to the Law Society Gazette. The charity has urged the government to reconsider and warned of further cuts. Chief executive Emma Taylor said the reduction would leave more litigants without help. Lord Neuberger, a patron, backed the call.
stories.hook: Support Through Court is closing two Essex services after a £300,000 Ministry of Justice funding cut

stories.title: Nvidia, CEO face shareholder class action over alleged investor deception
Crown Law’s Leadership Fight Turns Personal as Deputy Lodges Grievance Against Solicitor-General
stories.ltme_summary: Deputy Solicitor-General Madeleine Laracy has reportedly lodged a personal grievance against Solicitor-General Anna Adams KC over the Crown Law restructure, according to The Post as relayed by LawFuel. The PSA union has also taken the matter to the Employment Relations Authority. Adams denies any breach and says the changes followed an independent review.
stories.hook: Crown Law deputy reportedly lodges grievance against Solicitor-General Anna Adams KC

stories.title: AI Is Moving Faster Than Corporate Governance, and Legal Teams Are Struggling to Keep Up
stories.ltme_summary: Diligent Institute and Wilson Sonsini released the Q4 2026 General Counsel Risk Index, based on about 200 senior legal leaders. It finds nearly 60 per cent believe AI adoption is outpacing governance, 41 per cent lack a basic AI governance framework, and board AI readiness averages 2.9 out of five. The survey is predominantly North American.
stories.hook: Nearly 60 per cent of legal leaders say AI adoption outpaces governance, Diligent survey finds

stories.title: AI Law Firms Circle The Warm Body of Weil Gotshal
stories.ltme_summary: Following Weil Gotshal & Manges partners' November 10 vote to dissolve, AI-native firm Crosby has bid for the firm's brand, trademark and selected internal data, according to TechCrunch, as reported by LawFuel. Scissero and Vetta are also reported to be interested in other assets. Financial terms are undisclosed, and client confidentiality and privilege may limit what can be acquired.
stories.hook: AI-native firms Crosby, Scissero and Vetta circle Weil's brand, data and precedents

stories.title: Why Adam Milstein Wants Americans to Follow the Foreign Money
Four-month suspension for barrister over antisemitic LinkedIn posts
stories.ltme_summary: The Bar disciplinary tribunal has suspended barrister Forz Khan for four months over five social media posts it found antisemitic or seriously offensive, including a LinkedIn post about a 'final solution'. The decision can be appealed, and the suspension takes effect if no appeal is lodged. He was also ordered to pay £2,880 in costs. The full reasoning has not been published.
stories.hook: Barrister Forz Khan suspended for four months over antisemitic LinkedIn posts

stories.title: Lord Chancellor outlines ambition for National Legal Service
stories.ltme_summary: Lord Chancellor Alex Norris set out his ambition for an integrated National Legal Service at the Bar Council annual conference, aiming for structural legal aid reform before the spending review expected in 2027. He said the government wants to explore how new technologies can support access to advice, and that the UK should be at the forefront of the next generation of technology.
stories.hook: Lord Chancellor Alex Norris pitches a National Legal Service that uses new technology

stories.title: Group action to target collapsed law firm’s family protection trusts
stories.ltme_summary: Addleshaw Goddard is preparing a no-win, no-fee group action over family protection trusts created by the collapsed Anglo-Scottish firm McClure, and has invited affected people to register interest. The claim will be brought in Scotland but cover the whole UK. Jones Whyte, which took on McClure's work, reported 18,840 FPT files at the point of administration in 2021. Victims of McClure Solicitors welcomed the move.
stories.hook: Addleshaw Goddard prepares UK group action over McClure family protection trusts

stories.title: Magistrates sanctioned over failure to treat others with respect
stories.ltme_summary: Two magistrates have been sanctioned following complaints about their conduct in court. Hilary Whiteway, of the Avon and Somerset bench, received a formal warning after the Judicial Conduct Investigations Office found her conduct fell short of expected standards of respect and courtesy. Edward Beaman, of the Lancashire bench, received formal advice over criticism of two advocates. Mr Justice Keehan issued both sanctions on behalf of the Lady Chief Justice and the Lord Chancellor.
stories.hook: Two magistrates sanctioned by the JCIO for discourteous conduct, one receiving a formal warning and one formal advice

stories.title: Serial litigant tried to juggle two hearings at the same time
stories.ltme_summary: An employment tribunal ordered litigant Raymond Bryce to pay £1,000 in costs after he double-booked hearings, one at the tribunal and one at Birmingham County Court. Judge Dimbylow let his discrimination claim against Stoke-on-Trent City Council continue, finding the conduct unreasonable but not grounds for strike-out. The judge said he knew what he was doing.
stories.hook: Serial litigant Raymond Bryce pays £1,000 costs for juggling two hearings

stories.title: Avoiding another Mazur – LSB outlines plans to review guidance for ‘consistency, legal accuracy and clarity’
stories.ltme_summary: The Legal Services Board has announced a review of guidance to avoid a repeat of the Mazur crisis, aiming at consistency, legal accuracy and clarity. The extract available is only the headline and a related Today's Conveyancer link about the SRA's reset to proactive, intelligence-led regulation, so the body of the LSB announcement is not visible here.
stories.hook: LSB opens review of legal regulators' guidance to avoid another Mazur-style crisis

Section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026: abortion offence pardons
stories.ltme_summary: The Ministry of Justice's guidance explains section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which took effect on 16 November 2026. It automatically pardons women convicted or cautioned for abortion offences relating to their own pregnancy and requires police and courts to delete or annotate related records of convictions, cautions, arrests and investigations where reasonably practicable.
stories.hook: MoJ guidance sets out how police and courts must delete abortion-related records from 16 November

stories.title: Women pardoned for abortion offences relating to their own pregnancy
stories.ltme_summary: The Ministry of Justice says women convicted or cautioned for abortion offences relating to their own pregnancy are automatically pardoned, with records to be removed from 16 November 2026. The change follows section 242 of the Crime and Policing Act 2026, which also covers arrests and investigations. Police and courts must update records, and women need take no action. BPAS welcomed the change.
stories.hook: Women cautioned or convicted over their own abortions are automatically pardoned from 16 November

stories.title: Microsoft 365 Service Disruption
stories.ltme_summary: Microsoft 365 is experiencing a service disruption, according to a notice carried by PracticeEvolve Group, which includes the SOS brand. Users may be unable to connect to several Microsoft 365 services, and sign-in, email, tasks and calendar may be slow or unavailable. Microsoft is investigating and posts updates on its service health page.
stories.hook: Microsoft 365 outage hits sign-in, email and calendar for law firms using PracticeEvolve systems

stories.title: Microsoft 365 Service Disruption
stories.ltme_summary: SOS Legal has relayed a Microsoft 365 service disruption notice dated 13 November 2026. The notice says users may be unable to connect to several Microsoft 365 services, with sign-in, email integration, tasks and calendar items possibly slow or unavailable. Microsoft is investigating and posts updates on its service health page.
stories.hook: SOS Legal relays a Microsoft 365 disruption notice covering sign-in, email and calendar
